newsitem.title: USA: Jewish leader wants Swiss financial gesture.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader wants Swiss financial gesture.

text.p: A Jewish leader will ask Switzerland on Wednesday to make "a good faith financial gesture" toward Holocaust victims before it begins a planned five-year inquiry into the extent of Swiss financial collaboration with the Nazis.

World Jewish Congress (WJC) President Edgar Bronfman will make public a call for "material restitution" that has been discussed privately with the Swiss government when he appears before a House of Representatives Banking Committee hearing, according to a text of his remarks obtained by Reuters.

Bronfman did not give a dollar figure but Swiss sources have said amounts of about $250 million have been discussed in several meetings between the Swiss government and the WJC. The group was asked by the late Israeli leader Yitzhak Rabin to negotiate the issue of unclaimed Jewish assets in Swiss banks.

In his prepared remarks, Bronfman said, "The time has come for the competent authorities to make a good faith financial gesture -- one that does not prejudice the outcome of any final settlement -- so that those who suffered so much may see in their lifetime some measure of justice done."
He added, "... the urgent demands of the ever-shrinking population of Holocaust survivors must be met immediately."

A Swiss Embassy spokesman on Tuesday said Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti went on record last week as saying Swizterland would not take any concrete measures on restitution before the government's official inquiry reported its findings -- a task that could take up to five years.

The Swiss parliament on Monday cleared the way for the start of the investigation into the country's financial dealings with the Nazis and the handling by Swiss banks of deposits made by Jews before and during the Holocaust.

Besides Bronfman, the House panel will also hear testimony from Thomas Borer, chief Swiss government spokesman on whether Swiss banks hold unclaimed assets of Holocaust victims. It will be the first time Borer has appeared before a U.S. congressional committee.

Swiss officials hope he will be able to counter months of negative publicity that has painted neutral Switzerland as a willing partner of the Germans, helping them dispose of gold and other asserts looted from occupied Europe and, after the war, helping the Nazis to export millions to Latin America.

Embassy spokesman David Vogelsanger said the publicity generated by the release of hundreds of documents from the U.S. National Archives had painted Switzerland as a satellite of the Nazis. He said it was the only country in continental Europe that remained a democracy throughout the war.

"During the war we were surrounded by Germany and German-occupied countries and we did make compromises in the economic field. Everybody understood that at the time, but in hindsight things looked different," he said.

New York Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, who heads the Senate Banking Committee, will also appear before the House committee to detail his accusations that Switzerland was a key player in the looting by Nazis of the wealth of Europe, from the assets of Jews to the theft of gold from the national treasuries of Belgium, France and the Netherlands.
In New York on Tuesday, D'Amato said he agreed the Swiss should make an immediate financial gesture toward Holocaust victims.
